summary:
South Sudan's Penal Code reaches gender presentation directly. Section 379 criminalises "any male person who dresses or is attired in the fashion of a woman" and carries up to three months' imprisonment. The provision turns on appearance alone: it requires no sexual conduct and no disclosure of identity, so a trans visitor presenting female is exposed in public rather than only in private.

The same code treats consensual same-sex sexual conduct as an "unnatural offense", defined as carnal intercourse against the order of nature, punishable by up to 10 years' imprisonment. Where the conduct is nonconsensual the maximum rises to 14 years.

United States State Department country reports for 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021 and 2022 each record that no authorities were reported to have enforced the same-sex conduct provision. Those reports describe no repeal, no moratorium and no prosecution; the statute remains on the books and the dress provision is reported alongside it in each of those years.

Security forces were reported to harass, arrest, detain, torture and beat LGBTQI+ persons across the period covered by those State Department reports, 2018 to 2022. In September 2017 the minister for Labour, Public Service and Human Resource Development, Gathoth Gatkuoth Hothnyang, stated that the government would order security forces to arrest LGBTQ persons and detain them until they procreate; no arrests on that basis were reported by the end of that year.

There is no hate-crime or anti-discrimination legislation protecting LGBTQ persons from harassment or abuse on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. The one exception noted is that, as of 2020, harassment of employees on those grounds is prohibited for oil and gas companies operating in the country.

Same-sex couples have no legal recognition, and same-sex marriage has been constitutionally banned since the 2011 Constitution. The 2022 State Department report found that most openly LGBTQI+ citizens had fled South Sudan because of actively hostile government rhetoric and action.

The country has no known LGBTQ-support organisations. Access for All, a community-based rights group, was raided by security forces in 2017 and its staff detained for several months before release without charge; the organisation was intimidated into closing and its executive director later left the country.
tangentialFactors:
The Non-Governmental Organisations Act (2016) bars organisations from contravening the country's sovereignty, institutions and laws. Because same-sex activity is illegal, this provision may prevent LGBTQ-supportive civic groups from operating.

Societal stigma is documented at a high level: the 2011 State Department report found "widespread" societal discrimination against gay men and lesbians, and later reporting describes continued stigmatisation among the broader population. Official rhetoric has reinforced this, with then-President Salva Kiir Mayardit stating in July 2010 that homosexuality is not in the "character" of Southern Sudanese people and would never gain support.

South Sudan's legal framework on dress and same-sex conduct resembles that of other states that retain colonial-era "unnatural offense" provisions, but the specific Section 379 dress offence and the 2017 ministerial detention statement distinguish its enforcement posture.
localsOnly:
Residents face the same Section 379 dress provision and the "unnatural offense" penalties described for visitors, but with the added exposure of indefinite residence: no enforcement reports exist for the conduct offence across 2018 to 2022, yet security forces were reported to harass, arrest, detain, torture and beat LGBTQI+ persons during that period.

Employment protection on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity exists only within oil and gas companies as of 2020; no broader workplace or housing protection is in force.

Civic organising is constrained by the NGO Act (2016), and the documented closure of Access for All in 2017 after a security force raid illustrates the practical risk to residents who attempt to build support structures.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not document any enforcement of Section 379 itself; the State Department reports address non-enforcement of the same-sex conduct provision, and no prosecution under the dress provision is sourced here either way.

No data is available in this inventory on document or marker rules for trans South Sudanese citizens, on entry or visa screening of trans travellers, or on access to gender-affirming healthcare.

The inventory does not indicate whether the 2017 ministerial detention statement was ever formalised into an order or carried out after year's end.
